## Details on Broadcasted Operators {.unnumbered}


### Description

This help page gives some additional information on the properties of
the <code>bc.</code> functions and the overloaded operators. <br />
<br />



### Available Overloads

Sometimes broadcasting is needed in large mathematical expression,
involving multiple variables,
where precedence is of importance. <br />
For example in an expression like <code>x + y / z^y</code>. <br />
For such cases, you may want to overload the base operators. <br />
<br />
To that end, the 'broadcast' package provides the [broadcaster](broadcaster.qmd) class,
which comes with its own method dispatch for the base operators. <br />
If at least one of the 2 arguments of the base operators has the <code>broadcaster</code> class attribute,
and no other class (like <code>bit64</code>) interferes,
broadcasting will occur in the same manner as used in the various <code>bc.</code> - functions. <br />
<br />
The following arithmetic operators have a 'broadcaster' method:
+, -, *, /, ^, %%, %/% <br />
The following relational operators have a 'broadcaster' method:
==, !=, &lt;, &gt;, &lt;=, &gt;= <br />
And finally, the &amp; and | operators also have a 'broadcaster' method. <br />
<br />



### Attribute Handling

The <code>bc.</code> functions and the overloaded operators generally do <b>not</b>
preserve attributes, unlike the base 'R' operators. <br />
<br />
Broadcasting often results in an object with more dimensions, larger dimensions,
and/or larger length than the original objects. <br />
Therefore, the <code>names</code>, <code>dimnames</code>, and <code>dim</code> attributes often no longer fit the new object. <br />
Moreover, some classes are only appropriate for certain dimensions or lengths. <br />
Custom matrix classes, for example, presumes an object to have exactly 2 dimensions. <br />
And the various classes provided by the 'bit' package have length-related attributes. <br />
So even class attributes cannot be guaranteed to hold for the resulting objects. <br />
<br />
However, the <code>bc.</code> functions and the overloaded operators
<b>always</b> preserve the &quot;broadcaster&quot; attribute,
as this is necessary to chain together broadcasted operations. <br />
Notice that this contrats with base 'R' in the following sense: <br />
In base 'R', logical (&amp;, |) and relational (==, !=, etc.) operators never preserve attributes,
whereas the broadcasted equivalents do preserve the &quot;broadcaster&quot; attribute. <br />
<br />
Almost all functions provided by 'broadcast' are S3 or S4 generics; <br />
methods can be written for them for specific classes,
so that class-specific attributes can be supported when needed. <br />
<br />
Unary operations (i.e. <code>+ x</code>, <code>- x</code>) return the original object,
with only the sign adjusted. <br />
<br />
<br />



### Examples
```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=TRUE, collapse = TRUE, comment = NA}
library("broadcast")


# maths ====

x <- 1:10
broadcaster(x) <- TRUE

y <- 1:10
broadcaster(y) <- TRUE

x + y / x
x + 1 # mathematically equivalent to the above, since x == y
(x + y) / x
2 * x/x # mathematically equivalent to the above, since x == y

dim(x) <- c(10, 1)
dim(y) <- c(1, 10)

x + y / x
(x + y) / x

(x + y) * x


# relational operators ====
x <- 1:10
y <- array(1:10, c(1, 10))
broadcaster(x) <- TRUE
broadcaster(y) <- TRUE

x == y
x != y
x < y
x > y
x <= y
x >= y



```
